concept.name: Vega
concept.definition: Vega is the sensitivity of an option's price to a one-point change in the underlying's implied volatility: the partial derivative of option value with respect to volatility. All long options have positive vega; vega is largest for at-the-money options with longer time to expiration.
concept.intuition: Vega tells you how much your option's price inflates or deflates when the market's forecast of future movement changes, even if the stock itself hasn't moved.
concept.mechanics: Vega = dV/d(sigma), typically quoted per 1 percentage point of implied volatility; identical for calls and puts at the same strike in Black-Scholes. Positions long options are long vega and gain when implied volatility rises; short premium positions are short vega and suffer in volatility spikes. Vega decays toward zero as expiration approaches.
concept.formula: Vega = dV/d(sigma); Black-Scholes: Vega = S * N'(d1) * sqrt(T) (per unit vol; divide by 100 per vol point).
concept.failure_modes: Vega assumes a parallel shift of a single volatility number, but real surfaces move by strike and tenor, so vega-neutral books can still lose to skew or term-structure twists. The classic failure is 'volatility crush': a long option loses through vega after an event even when the directional call was right.
concept.misconceptions: Vega is not a Greek letter — the name is a market coinage (the symbol derives from a misread nu). Nor is implied volatility a forecast in the statistical sense; it is a price, so vega P&L reflects changes in option market pricing, not realized outcomes.
concept.example: A 60-day ATM call worth $4.00 with vega 0.12 rises to about $4.12 if implied volatility rises from 20% to 21%, with the stock unchanged; a short straddle with vega -0.25 loses $25 per vol point per contract.

citations.source: The Options Industry Council (OCC) — Understanding Options Greeks
